extracted.intended_audience: early 18th-century British reading public (gentlemen and ladies)
extracted.subtask_description: Short literary essays offering moral, social, and aesthetic guidance (manners, domestic conduct, taste in art and poetry) aimed at a polite early-18th-century readership. Contains prescriptive remarks about behaviour, economics, painting, ballads, and physiognomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female domestic virtues / proper province of women
rubrics_metrics.description: Women should 'endeavour to outshine' others in accomplishments proper to their sex, and 'distinguish themselves as tender Mothers, and faithful Wives, rather than as furious Partizans.' 'Female Virtues are of a Domestick Turn. The Family is the proper Province for Private Women to shine in.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid public partisan behaviour; cultivate domestic duties and modesty. Emphasises modest, private virtues over public political contention for women; appeals to classical examples (Greeks forbidding women at Olympic Games) as support.

rubrics_metrics.name: If showing public zeal, direct it against open enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: When women (or private persons) display public spirit, it should be aimed 'not against those who are perhaps of the same Family, or at least of the same Religion or Nation, but against those who are the open, professed, undoubted, Enemies of their Faith, Liberty and Country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid internecine or factional zeal; if sacrificing personal goods for public causes (e.g. contributing jewellery), such acts are laudable and may earn public recognition (e.g. permission for public orations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in expenditure and avoidance of debt
rubrics_metrics.description: Men should be wary of running into debt: extravagance and keeping up a false retinue lead to loss of honour, liberty, and fortune; a debtor is 'in that Condition with relation to twenty different People.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live within a modest compass of business; keep personal affairs simple so as to avoid temptations to excessive expense; be aware creditor powers (reputation, arrest). Antipatterns: keeping up appearances, gambling on reputation, extravagant living after a windfall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being surety / excessive credulity for others' debts
rubrics_metrics.description: Being a surety for others and believing all pretended demands destroy one's estate: 'This Easiness and Credulity destroy all the other Merit he has.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not act as guarantor for others or be so open-handed that others can take advantage; such behaviour commonly reduces estates and reputation. Example: Jack Truepenny, whose fortune was ruined by trusting others and acting as surety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and careful business dealings are laudable
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentleman who never was defendant in a law-suit and whose dealings give no colour for complaint (Sir Andrew) is praised as 'laudable' and uncommon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value steady, honest trading and scrupulous business conduct; contrasted with those who run into suits and debts through vice or imprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial, uniform smirking and flashy affectation in portraits (Vanity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanity's pictures are 'very remarkable for their Smiles, and a certain smirking Air which he bestowed indifferently on every Age and Degree of either Sex... every Part of the Dress was in a Flutter, and endeavoured to distinguish itself above the rest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: portraits that give every sitter the same affected grin, gaudy drapery, and glaring colours. Such mannerism produces superficial, insincere representations and should be avoided by artists and praised less by critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of slavish imitation (Stupidity copying Vanity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A labouring workman who 'copied after' Vanity and produced slavish imitations (called STUPIDITY).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of mere imitation: copying an affected mode without original judgment leads to inferior work. Artists should avoid unthinking mimicry of fashionable affectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of grotesque distortions and chimera (Fantasque)
rubrics_metrics.description: FANTASQUE 'had an excellent Hand at a Chimera, and dealt very much in Distortions and Grimaces... the most elaborate of his Pieces was at best but a terrifying Dream' — 'agreeable Monsters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grotesque invention and exaggerated distortions can produce striking effects but tend toward terrifying or monstrous results; their value is limited and they are not a substitute for true representation. Use with caution and awareness of audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hasty execution; do not let beauty fade (Avarice / haste)
rubrics_metrics.description: AVARICE had a 'hasty Hand, which left his Pictures so unfinished, that the Beauty... faded sooner than in the Person after whom it was drawn. He made so much haste... that he neither gave himself time to clean his Pencils, nor mix his Colours.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative example: rushing work destroys lasting beauty. Encourage deliberate workmanship, proper preparation and finishing; hastiness results in works that age poorly and betray the sitter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value industrious, meticulous workmanship and fidelity to detail (Industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: INDUSTRY 'did not omit a single Hair in his Face; if the Figure of a Ship, there was not a Rope among the Tackle that escaped him... Night-pieces... seemed to shew themselves by the Candles.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive criterion: careful, thorough labour produces convincing detail and realistic effects. Such industriousness yields durable, impressive pictures; praised over flashy but shallow techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-retouching that exaggerates defects (Envy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A workman who 'retouch[ed] the finest Pieces, tho' he produced no Originals of his own. His Pencil aggravated every Feature that was before over-charged, loaded every Defect, and poisoned every Colour it touched.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: needless retouching that amplifies flaws rather than improving the work. Critics/retouchers should refrain from altering originals to emphasize defects; restraint is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate the mellowing, improving effects of Time on works of art
rubrics_metrics.description: TIME, represented as an old Workman, 'wore off insensibly every little disagreeable Gloss... added such a beautiful Brown to the Shades, and Mellowness to the Colours, that he made every Picture appear more perfect than when it came fresh from the Master's Pencil.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that ageing can improve tonal harmony and remove harshness; older masters' works may gain depth and mellowness that early finishes lack. Critics should account for time's corrective effects when judging works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value simplicity and fidelity to nature in ballads and folk-poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The old ballad 'Two Children in the Wood' is praised as 'a plain simple Copy of Nature, destitute of the Helps and Ornaments of Art' whose 'Sentiments appear genuine and unaffected' and therefore move readers despite 'mean' language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive criterion for popular/folk verse: natural, unaffected sentiment and incidents appropriate to the subject (which 'grow out of the Subject') are more important than polished language or artifice. Critics should distinguish genuine simplicity from mere incompetence; true simplicity moves the humane reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of expression can be preferable to technical artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the ballad's language is 'mean,' the naturalness of thought makes it pleasing; 'those who are not Judges of Language' or who have 'a true and unprejudiced Taste of Nature' will be moved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss works solely for coarse diction; assess whether sentiment and natural expression compensate. Appeals to classical models (Horace, Moliere) indicate that great taste can admire nature in simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy: the air of the face conveys character more than lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay asserts that 'the Air of the whole Face is much more expressive than the Lines of it' and that 'the Air is generally nothing else but the inward Disposition of the Mind made visible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging temperament, attend to overall expression ('air') and the dynamic motions of countenance rather than isolated features; be aware that passions manifest visibly. Caveat: rules of physiognomy that fix feature-to-character correspondences are speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral injunction: be honest regardless of physiognomic appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: While physiognomy may incline people to form judgments, 'nothing can be more glorious than for a Man to give the Lie to his Face, and to be an honest, just, good-natured Man, in spite of all those Marks and Signatures which Nature seems to have set upon him for the Contrary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage moral action that counters prejudiced readings of appearance: personal virtue is superior to physiognomic expectation; do not excuse vice on the basis of 'brutal' or unfavorable looks.
